label: prop:qbeta-counit-closed-form
title: Closed form of the counit $Q$-value $\varepsilon(\Delta)\cdot\mathfrak{E}_0$
html:
Proposition. Closed form of the counit Q-value \varepsilon(\Delta)\cdot\mathfrak{E}_0

Let \Delta = \mathrm{NF}(n) - \mathrm{NF}(p) be the single-wrap normal-form difference of the neutron and proton typed-crossing elements in H_3(q), and write h = q - q^{-1}. Let \varepsilon denote the coordinate-sum functional \sigma \mapsto 1 (see the scope section below — it is not a counit) and \mathfrak{E}_0 = m_e/(q(q-1)) the per-Hecke-step energy scale. Then:

  \varepsilon(\Delta)\cdot\mathfrak{E}_0
  \;=\;
  \frac{m_e\,(q+1)(q^2 - 2q - 1)}{2q^3}.

Counit versus Markov trace

Two canonical functionals act on this difference:

  \varepsilon(\Delta) = \frac{h^2}{2} - h,
  \qquad
  \mathrm{tr}_M(\Delta) = \frac{h^2}{2} - h\,z.

On \Delta the coordinate sum agrees with the Markov trace at the trivial loop value z = 1, and the trivial-loop value is never attained on the substrate, so the two are genuinely distinct functionals there.

That agreement is a property of \Delta, not an identity. The Markov trace at z = 1 weights the standard basis as [1,1,1,1,1,h+1], while the coordinate sum weights it as [1,1,1,1,1,1], so

  \mathrm{tr}_M\big|_{z=1} - \varepsilon \;=\; h \cdot (\text{the } e^- \text{ coordinate}).

The two therefore coincide exactly on elements whose e^- coordinate vanishes, which both nucleon models happen to satisfy. The identity must not be quoted in general.

Scope: \varepsilon is not a counit, and is inadmissible under convention D

This statement is a construction in a non-canonical frame. Three separate points, each measured; none of them moves a number above.

It is not a counit. A unital algebra map into a commutative ring is automatically cyclic, hence a class function. The functional here is the coordinate sum \sigma \mapsto 1, which is not multiplicative: pushing the Hecke relation \sigma^2 = h\sigma + 1 through such a map forces h = 0. Formalized sorry-free as QOU.QBeta.CounitSigmaOne.h_eq_zero_of_image_one. The multiplicative functional the name suggests is the augmentation \sigma \mapsto q, which is a different map and gives a different value on the same vector.

It does not descend to the algebra the canonical convention places the theory in. Under convention D the trace ideal is the Temperley–Lieb radical, and the GNS space is H_\infty(q)/\mathcal{N} \cong \mathrm{TL}_\infty(q), not H_\infty(q). A functional descends to a quotient exactly when it annihilates the ideal. The augmentation annihilates J_{(1^3)}; the coordinate sum does not. Since \Delta has a non-zero (1^3) component, \varepsilon assigns different values to two representatives of the same class.

The admissible set is closed at two, and both miss. The descent condition y_{(1^3)}(z) = 0 is quadratic with roots z = q and z = z_D = q^3/(q^2+1); at z = q the Markov trace is the augmentation, so the two roots give two functionals, not three. Evaluated on the same vector against the measured Q-value, the augmentation gives +12.470\% and the Markov trace at z_D gives -43.157\%, while the coordinate sum used here gives +0.168\% at z = 1 — a loop value that is neither root. The functional that reproduces the measurement is the one the canonical convention forbids. The two admissible values bracket the target, so some convex combination reproduces it exactly; that is one parameter against one anchor, and any such weight must be derived from the representation rather than fitted.

Scope-(a) throughout: none of this shows the Q-value wrong. It records which functional the construction evaluates, and that it is excluded by the canonical convention. See beans qou-99qc (the open decision), qou-xzrj (the residual), and docs/audits/2026-08-26-qbeta-epsilon-is-inadmissible-under-convention-d.md.

Factorization of the energy scale

The per-Hecke-step energy factors through the information speed c_q^2 = 1/(q-1)^2 and the action-per-tick \hbar_q^{E} = (q-1)/q:

  \mathfrak{E}_0
  =
  \frac{m_e}{q(q-1)}.

The quantity \hbar_q^{E} is the energy-scale action quantum, distinct from the Hecke parameter h.
